segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And you were dead in your offenses and sins,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in which you once walked according to the age of this world, according to the ruler of the domain of the air, the spirit that is now at work in the sons of disobedience.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Among them we too all once lived in the desires of our flesh, carrying out the wishes of the flesh and of our thoughts, and we were by nature children of wrath, just like the rest.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But God, being rich in mercy, because of the great love with which he loved us,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: even when we were dead in our offenses, made us alive together with Christ—by grace you have been saved—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and raised us up with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that in the coming ages he might display the surpassing riches of his grace in kindness toward us in Christ Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not from yourselves; it is God’s gift—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: not from works, so that no one may boast.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we are his handiwork, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared in advance so that we would walk in them.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore remember that once you, the Gentiles in the flesh—called “the uncircumcision” by what is called “the circumcision,” made in the flesh by hands—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: remember that at that time you were apart from Christ, excluded from citizenship in Israel and foreigners to the covenants of the promise, having no hope and without God in the world.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But now in Christ Jesus you who once were far off have been brought near by the blood of Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For he himself is our peace, who made both one and broke down the dividing wall of the barrier, the hostility, in his flesh,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: nullifying the law of commandments set out in decrees, so that he might create the two in himself into one new person, making peace,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and might reconcile both to God in one body through the cross, having put the hostility to death by it.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he came and proclaimed the good news of peace to you who were far off, and peace to those who were near;

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: for through him we both have access in one Spirit to the Father.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, you are no longer foreigners and resident aliens, but you are fellow citizens with the holy ones and members of God’s household,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: built on the foundation of the apostles and prophets, with Christ Jesus himself as the cornerstone,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in whom the whole building, fitted together, grows into a holy sanctuary in the Lord,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: in whom you too are being built together into a dwelling place for God in the Spirit.

notes.note: The word means a wrongful act against God or another person. “Trespass” now chiefly suggests entering property without permission, so “offense” is used; the meaning itself is not disputed. It stands here beside the more general word “sins” with little difference in sense.

The Greek has the time-word “age” followed by the ordinary word for “world,” an unusual pairing. Most translations smooth it to “the course of this world” or “the ways of this world.” The literal form is kept here because it reflects the Jewish contrast between the present age and the age to come (compare verse 7). A minority of scholars have taken “Age” as the name of a personal power, but this is not widely accepted.

notes.phrase: the ruler of the domain of the air, the spirit
notes.traditional: the prince of the power of the air, the spirit
notes.note: The word usually rendered “power” or “authority” here most likely means the sphere over which authority is exercised, hence “domain.” The air was commonly thought of as the region where hostile spirits lived. In Greek “the spirit” is in the genitive case, so it may mean the ruler himself, or it may be a second thing he rules (“ruler of the domain of the air, of the spirit now at work”). The translation follows the more common reading.

The Greek pronoun is neuter, while “grace” and “faith” are both feminine nouns. Most scholars therefore take “this” to refer to the whole event of being saved by grace through faith. An old and still-held reading takes faith in particular to be what is called God’s gift.
The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples.” In the plural, in Jewish usage, it means the non-Jewish peoples. It is the same word translated “nations” elsewhere in the New Testament.

The word can mean either a body of citizens (a state or “commonwealth”) or the status and rights of a citizen. Many translations choose “commonwealth.” “Citizenship” is used here because verse 19 answers this verse with the related word “fellow citizens.” Either way, the point is that Gentiles stood outside the people to whom God’s promises belonged.

notes.phrase: the dividing wall of the barrier
notes.note: Many interpreters see an allusion to the stone balustrade in the Jerusalem temple, which carried inscriptions warning non-Jews not to pass it on pain of death. Others take the wall as an image for the Law of Moses, which was sometimes described as a fence around Israel. The two are not mutually exclusive, and the reference is uncertain.

notes.traditional: having abolished in his flesh the enmity, even the law of commandments
notes.note: The Greek syntax across verses 14 and 15 can be construed in more than one way. “The hostility” may explain the dividing wall that was broken down, as here, or it may be the object of the following verb, alongside the law (“nullifying in his flesh the hostility, the law of commandments”). “In his flesh,” which refers to Christ’s death, can likewise go with either verb. The translation keeps the Greek word order so that both readings remain possible.

The verb means to deprive something of force or effect, not to destroy it. Most translations have “abolished” or “set aside.” “Nullify” is used throughout this translation where the validity of a law or promise is at stake; the same verb appears in Romans 3:31, where Paul denies that faith nullifies the law. Scholars debate whether the law as a whole is meant here or the law in its role of dividing Jew from Gentile.

notes.phrase: proclaimed the good news of peace
notes.note: The verb is the ordinary Greek word for announcing good news and is related to the noun traditionally rendered “gospel.” The verse echoes Isaiah 57:19 (“peace, peace to the far and to the near”) and Isaiah 52:7 (the messenger who announces peace). In Isaiah the “far” are probably Jews in exile; here they are the Gentiles.

“Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. The Greek term is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Some interpreters think it refers here specifically to Jewish believers, or to angels, but most take it as God’s people as a whole.

The word comes from Isaiah 28:16 in the Greek version, where it describes a stone laid in a foundation. That is the majority understanding here, where the image is of a building rising from its foundation. Some scholars argue instead for the capstone or keystone that completes a structure at the top.

Greek has two words that English Bibles usually both translate “temple”: one for the whole complex with its courts, and this one for the building where God dwells. “Sanctuary” is used for the latter throughout this translation to keep the distinction; most versions have “a holy temple” here. The image is of the community as the place where God lives, as verse 22 makes explicit.

candidates.reason: It ranges from the physical body (verses 11, 14) to the Pauline sense of human nature opposed to God (verse 3), and versions vary between “flesh,” “sinful nature” and “human nature.”
The figurative sense “conduct one’s life” recurs throughout Paul and John; translators split between “walk” and “live,” and a fixed choice preserves links such as verses 2 and 10 here.
A central term across the letters, where “grace,” “favor” and “gift” are all defensible and inconsistent rendering would obscure a key theme.
It covers rescue, healing and salvation across the Gospels and letters, and needs a consistent policy on when “save” gives way to “heal” or “rescue.”
It means authority, the right to act, a domain of rule, or a class of spiritual powers; without one decision the renderings at Ephesians 1:21, 2:2, 3:10, 6:12 and Colossians 1:13 will drift.
